questions.q: What does an SCD Type 3 change do?
options: Overwrites the current value but captures it into a new 'previous value' column on the same row, keeping the same surrogate key
Inserts a brand-new row with a new surrogate key, like Type 2
Deletes the row entirely and reloads it from scratch
Never updates the attribute under any circumstances
questions.explain: Type 3 keeps a single row per dimension member, but adds an extra column that captures the immediately previous value at the moment the current value is overwritten.

questions.q: In the real Microsoft diagram used in this lesson, what happens to salesperson Lynn Tsoflias's row when her sales region changes from 4 to 5?
options: The row keeps the same surrogate key; SalesRegion_FK becomes 5, and new PreviousSalesRegion_FK / PreviousSalesRegionEndDate columns capture the old value and when it changed
A brand-new row is inserted with a new surrogate key
Her record is flagged with IsCurrent = FALSE and a new row is added
Nothing changes — Type 3 ignores the update entirely
questions.explain: This is the defining Type 3 mechanic: same row, same key, current value overwritten, but the prior value is captured into a sibling column rather than lost or moved to a new row.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe Type 3 as tracking "limited" history?
options: A Type 3 column only ever holds one prior value — if the attribute changes again, the earlier previous value is lost
Type 3 can only be used on numeric columns
Type 3 only works for dimensions with fewer than 100 rows
Type 3 history is limited to exactly 24 hours
questions.explain: Because there's only one 'previous' column, a second change overwrites it — Type 3 cannot reconstruct a full timeline the way Type 2 can.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does Microsoft's own guidance say about SCD Type 3?
options: It isn't commonly used, partly because it's difficult to use in a semantic model, and Type 2 is often recommended as a better fit
It should always be preferred over Type 2 for every attribute
It is the newest and most widely recommended SCD type
Microsoft's documentation never discusses SCD Type 3 at all
questions.explain: Microsoft's dimensional modeling documentation explicitly calls Type 3 uncommon and suggests considering whether Type 2 would be a better fit before implementing it.

questions.q: When does Type 3 genuinely earn its place over Type 2, according to this lesson?
options: When a report only needs to compare the current value against the immediately previous one, directly on the same row, without a self-join
When a full historical timeline of every change is required
When the attribute changes multiple times per day
Type 3 never has a legitimate use case over Type 2
questions.explain: Type 3's advantage is answering a narrow "current vs. immediately previous" comparison in a single row — a case where Type 2 would require joining across multiple versioned rows.
